title: Best Biking Day Trips Around Amsterdam
excerpt: Six rides beyond the canal ring — dikes, forests, windmills and one very windy beach — each an easy day out from Amsterdam Centraal.

children.text: There is a moment on almost every ride out of Amsterdam when the city simply lets go of you. The last tram stop slides past, the buildings get lower, a heron stands in a ditch as if it has been waiting for a bus since Tuesday, and suddenly the sky is enormous. I have lived here for years and that moment still catches me off guard.

It is also the best argument I know for owning a bike you actually like. Commuting teaches you the city; day trips teach you the country around it. You pack a sandwich, you leave when you feel like it, and you come home a little sunburnt and slightly smug. Nobody has ever regretted a day spent pedalling towards a windmill.
A note on numbers: every distance below is measured
as the crow flies

from Amsterdam Centraal. Crows do not stop for bridges, traffic lights or apple cake, so expect the real ride to be a fair bit longer. The Trip Planner at the bottom of this page does the maths for you and suggests which Red Panda to take. For anything over about 5 km it will nudge you towards an E-Bike, which is advice you are free to ignore until the wind picks up.
Six rides worth a whole day
1. Amstelpark — 5.3 km

The gentlest ride on the list, and a good one for a first outing or a lazy Sunday. Head south out of the centre and follow the Amstel as it widens and the houseboats get more elaborate, then cut west through Zuid. Almost all of it is on red asphalt bike paths, well away from cars, with plenty of excuses to stop for coffee.

Amstelpark was laid out for a garden exhibition in the early 1970s, and it still feels like someone's very ambitious back garden. There is a rose garden that smells wonderful in June, a hedge maze that is more confusing than it has any right to be, and a miniature train that small children treat as a serious form of transport. Bring a book. Lie on the grass. Nobody is timing you.
Tip: on the way back, follow the Amstel to the Riekermolen, the old windmill on the riverbank where a bronze Rembrandt stands sketching. It turns a short ride into a proper afternoon.
2. Durgerdam — 7.3 km

Ride east through the old docklands and cross the water to Schellingwoude, where the road climbs onto the dike along the IJmeer and the city falls away almost at once. On one side there is water all the way to the horizon; on the other, meadows, cows and the occasional very judgemental goose.

Durgerdam is a single row of wooden houses strung along the dike, painted in greens and whites and the occasional brave yellow, some of them leaning at angles that suggest a long relationship with the weather. It was a fishing village once, and it still has that quiet, salty feel. There is a small harbour, a café terrace facing the water, and a lot of benches placed by people who clearly understood the view. Sit on one for longer than you planned.
Tip: bring a layer, even in July. The wind off the IJmeer is real, it has opinions, and it will share them with you all the way home.
3. Amsterdamse Bos — 8.6 km

Amsterdam's forest is not a park with a few trees in it. It is a proper wood, roughly three times the size of Central Park, planted by hand in the 1930s on flat reclaimed land and now thick enough to get pleasantly lost in. Ride south-west through Oud-Zuid, past the Olympic Stadium, and within half an hour you have swapped traffic lights for birdsong.

Cyclists get their own network of paths inside. Start with a lap of the Bosbaan, the long, dead-straight rowing course where crews glide up and down while their coaches shout at them from bikes on the bank. Then head for the goat farm, where the kids (both kinds) are the main attraction and the adults are allowed to pretend they only came for the coffee. On a warm day the shade under the beeches feels like a small miracle.
Tip: have pancakes at the farm café, and go early on weekends. By noon on a sunny Saturday half of Amsterdam has had exactly the same idea.
4. Zaanse Schans — 12.0 km

This is the ride where the postcard version of Holland turns out to be real. Take the free ferry behind Centraal across to Noord, head north through Zaandam, then follow the river Zaan as it winds past old warehouses and factories that once smelled of cocoa and mustard. On the right day some of them still do, which is a very good reason to ride slowly.

Zaanse Schans is a small neighbourhood of green wooden houses and working windmills lined up along the water. They are not decorations: some still grind spices, press oil or saw timber, and in a few you can climb inside and feel the whole building creak as the sails go round. Park the bike, walk the dike, and try not to take four hundred photos of the same mill. You will fail. Everyone does.
Tip: arrive before 10:00, ahead of the tour buses. You get the windmills, the mist on the river and the clog workshop more or less to yourself.
5. Marken — 16.3 km

Take the ferry to Noord and ride out into Waterland, a flat, green patchwork of meadows and narrow ditches where the loudest thing is usually a lapwing. Pass through Broek in Waterland, with its immaculate wooden houses, and on to Monnickendam, a harbour town that deserves a coffee stop of its own.

From there you roll onto the long dike that has joined Marken to the mainland since 1957. Before that it was an island, and it still behaves like one: dark green houses clustered on mounds to keep their feet dry, and a pace of life that makes Amsterdam feel frantic. Leave the bike near the harbour and walk the path out to the lighthouse, the one locals call Het Paard, with water on both sides and sky in every direction.
Tip: in summer a ferry runs from Marken to Volendam, so you can make a loop of it and ride home a different way.
6. Zandvoort Beach — 25.4 km

The big one. Head west out of the city and into Haarlem, which is lovely enough to be a destination on its own, then follow the signs to the coast. The last stretch takes you through the dunes of the Kennemerland national park, a rolling landscape of sand, pine and heather where you may spot Highland cattle grazing with complete indifference to your effort.

And then, with the smell of salt getting stronger, you crest one last dune and there it is: the North Sea, grey or blue depending on its mood, and a long line of beach cafés with their feet in the sand. Lock up, take your shoes off and walk straight into the water. It will be colder than you expect. It always is.
Tip: on a headwind day, this is where an E-Bike earns its keep. The wind here usually blows in from the sea, so the ride out can be a grind and the ride home a gift.
Before you go

5 things nobody tells you about riding in Amsterdam
first. Then pack:
Water, more than you think you need
Lights, front and back, in case the day runs long
A good lock, because windmills attract bike thieves too
The ferry times, especially for the IJ crossings and Marken
A spare layer, whatever the forecast promised
The best rides are the ones where you forget to check how far you have gone.
Whichever you choose, go slowly, stop often and eat something with apple in it. Pick a spot below to see how far it is from you — and which Red Panda we'd take.
